blocks.text: The Standard Model is the collection of theories that describe the smallest experimentally observed particles of matter and the interactions between energy and matter. Three categories of particles form the Standard Model (Fig. 12.8): quarks, leptons and the bosons. Matter, which makes up only about 5% of the universe, is composed of quarks and leptons. The fundamental bosons provide three forces: electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force and the weak nuclear force. The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012, explains how the other particles get mass.

blocks.alt: A chart in two parts. Fermions (matter): a purple panel of quarks and antiquarks, up, charm and top above down, strange and bottom, each paired with its antiquark; a green panel of leptons and antileptons, the electron, muon and tau neutrinos above the electron, muon and tau, each paired with its antiparticle. Bosons: photon, gluon, Z and W marked as force carriers, and the Higgs boson h below them.

blocks.long_description: Each antiparticle is a second disc behind and below its particle, its symbol written with a bar (anti-up u-bar, anti-down d-bar, the antineutrinos nu-bar) or, for the charged leptons, with a plus sign (e+, mu+, tau+).

blocks.title: Limits of the Standard Model
blocks.text: The model is still considered incomplete. Currently it is unable to explain many important features of the known universe, such as (i) gravity, (ii) dark matter (27% of the universe) and (iii) dark energy (68% of the universe).
